tina4-python/tests/fixtures/write_path_contract.json
tina4-php/tests/fixtures/write_path_contract.json
tina4-ruby/spec/fixtures/write_path_contract.json
tina4-nodejs/test/fixtures/write_path_contract.json
The WRITE-PATH contract - feature 3 of the feature audit.
This exists to make one specific change checkable: moving insert/update/
delete OUT of 6 Python, 10 PHP and 7 Node adapters and INTO one builder per
framework, the shape Ruby already has. That change is worth ~4.3x the code,
and it is the single most dangerous change in the audit, because a subtle
break in the write path does not throw - it writes the wrong rows.
So this suite pins the CURRENT behaviour BEFORE anything moves. Run it, then
move the builder, then run it again. If it does not pass identically on every
engine, the move is wrong.
RUN IT AGAINST EVERY LIVE ENGINE. SQLite alone proves nothing here: the whole
reason per-adapter SQL exists is that placeholder style, RETURNING support and
identifier quoting differ exactly where the engine differs. A green SQLite run
is the least informative possible result.
No mocks. A database is a real dependency and CI provisions it.
THE RUNNERS EXECUTE THIS FILE. Every case below runs in python, php, ruby and
node, driven by the same `name`, the same `op`, the same seed and the same
answer key - the shape adapter_contract.json and batch_write_contract.json
already use. This file used to be ORPHANED: nothing read it, the four runners
were hand-written independently, and they drifted to 17/16/15/14 cases with
different names. That is how `a_string_filter_with_params...` below was never
executed anywhere, while the bug it describes shipped: Node's postgres, mysql,
mssql and firebird adapters walked a string filter with Object.keys(), so
Object.keys("1 = 1") yielded ["0","1",...] and PostgreSQL answered
`column "0" does not exist`. Do not add a hand-written case to a runner - add
it HERE, so all four gain it at once.
OPS a runner must implement: insert, insert_batch, update, delete, truncate,
primary_key, transaction_rollback, transaction_commit, execute_raw.
EXPECTATIONS a runner must check:
affected_rows            - the write reported this many rows
rows_after               - the table holds this many rows when the op is done
unchanged                - one row matching EVERY listed column still exists
primary_key              - primary_key(table) reports exactly this list
last_id_is_set_or_null   - a last insert id, or null; never a stale value
last_id_is_not_stale     - the reported last id is NOT this earlier row's id
last_id_is_null          - last id is insert-only; update/delete report none
visible_after_reconnect  - a SECOND connection to the same database sees it
expect_raises            - the op raises rather than writing
expect_error_recorded    - the cause stays readable on get_error() after it
Each case starts from BOTH tables empty, applies its own seed, then runs its
op. Cases never depend on each other or on their order.

table.name: tina4_write_contract
table._note: Single-column primary key. Created and dropped by each runner. Ids come from the DATA, not a sequence - the cases name id 1 and 2 explicitly, and an identity column would fight them.
table.ddl: CREATE TABLE tina4_write_contract (id INTEGER NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(80), qty INTEGER)

composite_table.name: tina4_write_composite
composite_table._note: A primary key spanning TWO columns. Feature 4 found that a key was assumed to be one column, so a write keyed on only the first matched every row sharing that value. NOT NULL is explicit because a composite key column must be non-nullable on every engine.
composite_table.ddl: CREATE TABLE tina4_write_composite (tenant VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, code VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL, label VARCHAR(80), PRIMARY KEY (tenant, code))

cases.name: insert_reports_a_last_insert_id
cases._note: lastId is set on INSERT only. Engines that cannot report one (some ODBC paths, and any engine asked for a non-identity key) may return null; they must NOT return a stale id from an earlier write. The seeded row 1 is that earlier write, so its id must never come back as the id of the row just inserted.

cases.name: update_with_no_filter_uses_the_primary_key_from_the_data
cases._note: Feature 4: update() with no filter takes the PK out of the data and uses it as the WHERE clause. It does NOT rewrite every row. affected_rows must also never be 0 while a matching row exists - Node's old failure mode, where a caller who did not inspect the result believed the write landed.

cases.name: a_string_filter_with_params_updates_the_same_rows_as_a_hash_filter
cases._note: The update half of the two documented filter forms. Same seed and same answer key as update_with_an_explicit_filter_changes_only_matching_rows, spelled the other way; if the two ever disagree, one form is broken.

cases.name: a_string_filter_with_params_works_the_same_as_a_hash_filter
cases._note: Both forms are documented in all four; they must not diverge. THIS is the case no runner executed while the fixture was orphaned, and it is exactly the shape that was broken in four Node adapters.

cases.name: truncate_removes_every_row
cases._note: Emptying a table is a real thing to want, and it has to be spelled out - delete() with no filter raises. truncate() is the method that walks a raw '1 = 1' string filter into the adapter, which is how the Object.keys() bug was actually found.

cases.name: a_standalone_write_is_durable_without_an_explicit_commit
cases._note: The autocommit contract: ON for a standalone write. Verified by reading the row back on a DIFFERENT connection where the engine allows it.

cases.name: the_primary_key_is_introspected_rather_than_assumed
cases._note: primary_key() returns a LIST on every framework. A resolver that guessed 'id' would pass here and fail the composite case below - which is the point of having both.

cases.name: a_composite_primary_key_reports_every_key_column
cases._note: A key that collapsed to its first column would build WHERE tenant = ? and match every row in the tenant. That is the data-loss bug, one layer down from the write.

cases.name: a_composite_key_write_matches_on_every_key_column
cases._note: Feature 4's sharpest case. Two rows share `tenant`; a write keyed on tenant alone would hit both.

errors.name: update_with_neither_a_filter_nor_a_primary_key_raises
errors._note: Feature 4, breaking in 3.13.94: a write with no filter is an ERROR, not a full-table operation. This is the case that used to overwrite every row - so the seeded rows must still be exactly as seeded once it has raised.

errors.name: delete_with_no_filter_raises
errors._note: truncate() is the explicit whole-table spelling, and it is a different method on purpose.

errors.name: delete_with_a_blank_string_filter_raises
errors._note: A BLANK string is not a filter, it is the absence of one, and it must raise exactly like an empty hash. Node's guard skipped the emptiness test for anything typed string, so delete(t, "") fell through to the adapter, which renders an empty WHERE as `DELETE FROM t` - a silent whole-table delete through the one method that exists to make that impossible.

errors.name: update_with_a_blank_string_filter_and_no_primary_key_raises
errors._note: The update half of the same property: a blank string filter is no filter, so it falls through to the primary key - and with no PK in the data that is an error, not a full-table rewrite.

errors.name: a_composite_key_write_missing_part_of_the_key_raises
errors._note: Half a composite key is not a filter. Accepting it would match every row sharing the first column.

errors.name: execute_raises_on_a_bad_statement_and_never_returns_false
errors._note: The fail-loud contract. The cause stays readable on get_error() after the raise.

errors.name: facade_insert_on_constraint_violation_throws
errors._note: Feature 3/9 fail-loud gap, found Node-only during the seeder-28 pass: Database.insert() must raise on a real PRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE violation exactly like update()/delete()/execute() already do here, not swallow it into a `{success:false}` result. Node's SQLiteAdapter.insert() single-row path catches the driver error and returns `{success:false, affectedRows:0, error}` instead of throwing, and the facade passed that result through UNCHECKED (update()/delete()/truncate() already run it through the same assertWrote() check that adapterInsert() -- the seedTable()/seedOrm() helper -- already had; insert() was the one write method missing it). Proven on the SAME table every other case here uses, so the fixture needs no new column: inserting a second row whose id already exists collides on the PRIMARY KEY (the UNIQUE half of 'a real NOT NULL / UNIQUE violation').
